title: Learning to Program Alongside AI: Critical Thinking, AI Ethics, and Gendered Patterns of German Secondary School Students
venue: 2026 IEEE/ACM 48th International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE-SEET ’26)
extended_summary:
This paper examines how German secondary school students engage with generative AI in programming, focusing on two main questions: how they perceive their own critical thinking in AI-assisted programming and how they understand AI ethics and responsibility. The author positions the study as a response to a gap in prior research, which has focused largely on university students rather than younger learners encountering programming and GenAI at the same time. The paper also investigates whether these perceptions differ by gender.

The study uses a survey-based mixed-methods approach combining Likert-scale items with open-ended questions. Quantitative items were adapted from prior instruments on critical thinking and AI literacy, and qualitative responses were analyzed thematically. Rather than evaluating a learning intervention or comparing treatment conditions, the study documents students’ existing AI-assisted programming practices, including which GenAI tools they use, how often they use them, whether they trust generated code, how they seek help, and how they think about privacy, accountability, and regulation.

Participants were 84 German secondary school students aged 16–19 recruited from two extracurricular software development workshops, one lasting one day and one lasting five days. Students worked collaboratively on small software projects such as Java or Python games and App Inventor apps. All participants reported using GenAI tools for programming, especially ChatGPT, primarily for code generation and debugging. The context was extracurricular rather than regular classroom instruction, and workshop instructors did not provide guidance on AI use so that responses would reflect students’ independent habits.

The main conclusion is that students show an 'AI paradox': they report strong ethical awareness, support for transparency, regulation, testing, and accountability, yet many also report integrating AI-generated code they do not fully understand. Boys were more likely to consult AI before teammates and to use AI more frequently, while girls expressed greater skepticism and stronger emphasis on peer collaboration and accountability. The author argues that programming education should connect ethical awareness to concrete coding practice, for example through code explanation, documentation of AI use, and explicit support for critical AI literacy in culturally responsive software engineering education.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory mixed-method survey study with descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and qualitative thematic analysis, but no experimental or quasi-experimental comparison of learning outcomes. It provides useful empirical data yet meets only limited causal credibility criteria.
impact_tier_rationale: The study shows meaningful but mixed patterns in durable skills and ethics-related perceptions, with one medium-sized gender association (Cramer's V=.421) but no direct academic learning impact or broad causal effect estimate. Overall impact is informative but unclear for general K-12 outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI tools (primarily ChatGPT, also Gemini, Claude, Perplexity) used by German secondary students for AI-assisted programming tasks such as code generation, debugging, and code checking in extracurricular software development workshops.

finding.finding_summary: In a survey of 84 German secondary students aged 16–19 who all reported using GenAI for programming, students reported strong software-engineering-related critical thinking practices such as testing code even if others already tested it (88% agree/strongly agree), checking code for defects (86%), and evaluating alternative solutions (61%). However, a substantial minority reported risky practices, including using code they did not fully understand (21% agree/strongly agree; 32% neutral), and boys were significantly more likely than girls to ask GenAI before a teammate (chi-square(4)=10.448, p=.034, Cramer's V=.421, medium effect), indicating mixed implications for critical thinking and collaborative problem solving.
finding.measure: Self-report 5-point Likert survey items on critical thinking practices in AI-assisted programming (e.g., code comprehension, evaluating alternatives, defect checking, testing, help-seeking, trust in AI outputs), plus thematic analysis of open-ended responses
finding.effect_size: Cramer's V=0.421 for gender difference on AI-first help-seeking; other reported effects small/negligible

finding.finding_summary: Students showed strong endorsement of AI governance and accountability principles: 88% agreed GenAI should meet ethical and legal standards, 90% agreed users should be informed about purpose/how it works/limitations, and 95% agreed systems should undergo rigorous testing. Qualitative responses emphasized multi-stakeholder governance involving politics, companies, developers, and schools, suggesting substantial institutional and regulatory awareness in this German secondary cohort.
finding.measure: Self-report 5-point Likert survey items on AI ethics, accountability, transparency, fairness, and testing, plus thematic analysis of responsibility/governance open-ended responses
finding.effect_size: For gender difference on accountability item, chi-square(4)=9.684, p=.046, Cramer's V=.405; otherwise descriptive percentages only

finding.finding_summary: The paper descriptively reports gendered patterns in attitudes and engagement with GenAI-assisted programming rather than testing a direct intervention effect on motivation: boys were more likely to be daily AI users (48% of boys vs 21% of girls), while girls reported more cautious use and stronger preference for peer collaboration. These findings indicate mixed patterns of engagement and comfort with GenAI, but no validated motivation or engagement effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Self-reported AI tool usage frequency, attitudes toward trust and help-seeking, and qualitative descriptions of cautious versus experimental use
